# Abstract

The river basins of the Chao Phraya, the middle Mekong and the maritime corridors of the Kra Isthmus (783.386 km², encompassing 9.642 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) supported the demographic, political and agrarian transformation of central Mainland Southeast Asia across more than two millennia. From the late prehistoric iron-using communities of the Chao Phraya delta margin and the Mun-Chi river system to the emergence of early historic Mon Dvaravati urban nodes, the northern expansion of Khmer provincial outposts, the south-western migration of Tai-speaking populations, the consolidation of Sukhothai and Lan Na, the zenith of the Ayutthayan riverine empire and the Lao confederation of Lan Xang, regional settlement patterns evolved through a persistent dialogue between wet-rice hydraulics, monsoon fluctuations and maritime trade networks.

Reconstructed across six physiographic divisions from 500BC to 1769AD under MANDALA, regional population expanded from 950k inhabitants in 500BC to 1,45M in 500AD as iron-age agrarian intensification and initial maritime contact stimulated nucleated settlements along river terraces and coastal embayments. Population reached 2,15M in 1000AD during the flourishing of Dvaravati monastic centres and coastal transshipment ports, advancing to 2,95M in 1300AD as Tai principalities coalesced across the northern intermontane valleys and upper alluvial plains. With the maturation of intensive wet-rice broadcast farming, royal canal construction and international maritime commerce under Ayutthaya, regional population expanded to 3,9M in 1500AD and 4,75M in 1650AD, culminating at 5,1M inhabitants by 1769AD (yielding an aggregate regional density of 651,02 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic mass remained concentrated in the fertile alluvial lowlands of the Lower Chao Phraya basin. At the 1769AD benchmark, the Lower Chao Phraya accommodated 1,53M people (30% of regional population; attaining 1.423,65 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the metropolitan conurbation of Ayutthaya and Thonburi. The Khorat Plateau supported 918k inhabitants (18%; 533,82 persons per 100 km²) along the Mun and Chi floodplains. Lan Na and the northern intermontane valleys accommodated 765k people (15%; 763,79 persons per 100 km²), centred on Chiang Mai. The Upper Chao Phraya basin supported 714k people (14%; 777,13 persons per 100 km²), anchored by Sukhothai and Nakhon Sawan. The Lan Xang Mekong corridor housed 663k people (13%; 280,66 persons per 100 km²), linking Luang Prabang and Vientiane. The Peninsular Isthmus accommodated 510k people (10%; 673,85 persons per 100 km²), anchored by Nakhon Si Thammarat.

This historical demographic synthesis combines 850 catalogued settlement trajectories with systematic geoarchaeological records of deltaic progradation, epigraphic surveys and hydraulic engineering chronicles. By subtracting nucleated urban centres from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the reconstruction isolates administrative, monastic and mercantile populations from the surrounding agricultural countryside. The trajectory demonstrates that Southeast Asian political consolidation was fundamentally tethered to the management of wet-rice agricultural surpluses and the seasonal mobilization of manpower through the corvée and patron-client structures of the muang polity system.

# Background

## Riverine Geomorphology and Hydroclimatic Framework

The physical geography of central Mainland Southeast Asia is defined by three interconnected hydrological domains: the Chao Phraya River system, the middle Mekong River corridor and the maritime Isthmus of Kra [@Stark2020Landscapes]. The Chao Phraya basin occupies a structural depression flanked by the Tenasserim mountain spine to the west, the Phetchabun and Dong Phaya Yen ranges to the east and the northern highlands of the Daen Lao and Thanon Thong Chai ranges. Four primary northern tributaries - the Ping, Wang, Yom and Nan - drain intermontane valleys before coalescing at Nakhon Sawan to form the Chao Phraya trunk stream, which meanders southwards through a flat alluvial plain toward the Gulf of Thailand [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati].

During the late mid-Holocene, around 3000BC, marine transgression inundated the lower central plain, creating the Bangkok marine embayment that reached inland as far north as Ayutthaya [@Claude2019Recent]. Subsequent marine regression and rapid deltaic progradation over the first millennia BC and AD transformed coastal mangrove swamps into fertile freshwater alluvial plains crossed by shifting river distributaries and seasonal swamps [@Taweethong2023Early]. This dynamic fluvial ecology generated natural levees, backswamp depressions and annual flood pulses governed by the southwest monsoon between May and October, providing ideal conditions for deep-water floating rice and seasonal inundation agriculture [@Claude2019Recent].

East of the Chao Phraya basin, the Khorat Plateau forms an elevated sandstone tableland tilted gently toward the east, drained by the Mun and Chi rivers into the Mekong [@Murphy2015Many]. With thin, sandy soils and marked seasonal rainfall deficits caused by the rain shadow of the Annamite range, the Khorat Plateau necessitated specialised hydraulic adaptations, including seasonal water ponding, earth bund construction and the exploitation of salt deposits and iron ores [@Stark2020Landscapes; @Murphy2015Many]. To the north, the intermontane basins of Lan Na provided confined fertile floodplains enclosed by granite and limestone ranges, fostering localized community irrigation systems known as muang fai [@Stark2020Landscapes]. To the south, the narrow Kra Isthmus linked the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, creating vital overland transpeninsular portage routes along protected river estuaries such as Nakhon Si Thammarat and Patani [@Patnukao2024Tracing].

## Proto-Historic Agrarian Systems and Dvaravati Urbanism

During the late prehistoric period (ca. 500BC to 500AD), communities across the central plain and the Mun-Chi valleys transitioned from bronze-iron metallurgy to complex agrarian village networks [@Taweethong2023Early]. Archaeological investigations at Ban Chiang, Ban Non Wat and in the Bang Pakong Valley demonstrate the emergence of iron-tipped plough agriculture, specialized ceramic production and extensive trade in carnelian, glass beads and copper ingots [@Taweethong2023Early]. These communities occupied naturally elevated earthen mounds adjacent to seasonal watercourses, practicing bunded wet-rice farming and domesticating water buffalo to manage heavy alluvial clays.

Between the sixth and eleventh centuries AD, the Lower Chao Phraya basin became the geographic nucleus of the Dvaravati culture, an early historic civilization characterised by Mon-speaking populations, Theravada and Mahayana Buddhist institutions and Indic administrative terminology [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many]. Dvaravati settlements exhibited distinctive spatial morphologies:
1. Moated settlement layouts: circular, oval or irregular rounded earthen ramparts encircled by wide water-filled moats, exemplified by Nakhon Pathom, Ku Bua, U Thong, Lopburi (Lavo) and Muang Fa Daet on the Khorat Plateau [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many].
2. Buddhist monumental architecture: brick stupas, laterite terraces and colossal stone Dharmacakras (Wheels of the Law) associated with seated Buddha images, marking religious authority and state patronage [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati].
3. Hydraulic infrastructure: diversion canals and large storage reservoirs (barays) designed to store monsoon rainfall for urban consumption and domestic cultivation [@Stark2020Landscapes].

At Nakhon Pathom, the monumental Phra Pathom Chedi stood at the heart of an expansive moated enclosure covering over 3,7 km², supporting an urban population of 15k to 25k residents during its seventh to ninth century climax [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati]. Along the eastern margin of the central plain, Lavo (Lopburi) controlled trade routes connecting the Chao Phraya with the Khorat Plateau, serving as a primary administrative centre that mediated cultural contacts between Dvaravati and the rising Khmer Empire centered at Angkor [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many].

## The Rise of Northern Tai Polities and Sukhothai

From the eleventh to thirteenth centuries AD, Tai-speaking populations migrated southwards from the upland valleys of southern China and northern Indochina, penetrating the Ping, Kok, Yom and Nan river valleys [@Stark2020Landscapes]. Organized into cellular territorial units termed muang, each presided over by an aristocratic ruler (chao), Tai communities practiced sophisticated weir-and-channel irrigation (muang fai), enabling intensive wet-rice cultivation along narrow mountain terraces and floodplain fans [@Thailand2020Basic].

The thirteenth century witnessed the fragmentation of Khmer provincial dominance and the coalescence of independent Tai kingdoms [@Michael1991Khamhaeng]:
- Sukhothai: established in the mid-thirteenth century along the Yom River, Sukhothai expanded under King Ram Khamhaeng into an influential Theravada Buddhist kingdom [@Michael1991Khamhaeng]. The city developed complex water management features, including the Phra Ruang dam and extensive earthen barrages (saridphong) that channeled montane streams into urban reservoirs and temple precincts [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Thailand2024Promote].
- Si Satchanalai: located 55 km north of Sukhothai, this sister city became an international ceramic manufacturing hub, exporting thousands of glazed celadon ceramics (Sangkhalok ware) throughout Southeast Asia and the Japanese archipelago [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Thailand2025Effect].
- Lan Na: founded in 1296AD by King Mangrai in the fertile Chiang Mai-Lamphun basin along the Ping River, Lan Na integrated ancient Mon Hariphunchai traditions with Tai military organization, creating a stable northern confederation that endured for centuries [@Stark2020Landscapes; @Thailand2023Growth].

These northern Tai polities established a decentralized, concentric political model often conceptualized as a mandala system, wherein authority radiated outward from an urban core across tributary client principalities without rigid territorial boundaries [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Murphy2015Many].

## The Ayutthayan Hydraulic Empire and Lao Lan Xang

In 1351AD, King Uthong founded the city of Ayutthaya on an island at the confluence of the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak and Lopburi rivers [@Tangtenglam2023Developing]. This location combined three geographic advantages: exceptional agricultural fertility provided by annual silt deposition, immunity from prolonged military siege due to seasonal monsoon inundation, and deep-water maritime access allowing ocean-going junks to dock directly beneath city walls [@Tangtenglam2023Developing; @Claude2019Recent].

Ayutthaya rapidly evolved into one of the largest metropolitan capitals in early modern Asia [@Tangtenglam2023Developing]. The kingdom implemented extensive hydraulic engineering projects, excavating rectilinear canals across the island to serve as municipal thoroughfares, defensive moats and tidal drainage conduits [@Tangtenglam2023Developing]. By the seventeenth century, foreign travelogues by Dutch, French and Persian emissaries described a cosmopolitan metropolis of 200k to 300k inhabitants, surrounded by prosperous foreign trading quarters accommodating Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch, Persian and Malay merchants [@Tangtenglam2023Developing; @Patnukao2024Tracing].

The Ayutthayan agrarian state relied upon the phrai corvée system, legally obligating commoners to provide three to six months of unpaid labour annually to crown officials and noble patrons, facilitating massive canal excavations, city wall construction and royal military campaigns [@Thailand2020Basic; @Thailand2025Learning]. This administrative apparatus depended upon sophisticated clerical recording and royal tax ledgers managed through provincial visual administrative protocols [@Thailand2023Visible; @Thailand2025Visible].

Simultaneously, in the middle Mekong basin, King Fa Ngum established the unified Lao kingdom of Lan Xang (the Kingdom of a Million Elephants and the White Parasol) in 1354AD [@Murphy2015Many]. Centered initially at Luang Prabang (Muang Sua) and later relocated southwards to Vientiane in 1560AD by King Setthathirath to escape Burmese military incursions, Lan Xang commanded the riverine trade of the Mekong, linking the forested upland margins of Yunnan and the Annamite cordillera with the lowland agrarian basins of the south [@Murphy2015Many; @Thailand2024Strategies]. Provincial governors and local monastic leaders maintained community cohesion through decentralized administrative training packages and communal learning assemblies [@Thailand2024Training; @Thailand2023Innovative].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distribution across 783.386 km² of terrestrial surface, the MANDALA spatial engine partitions central Mainland Southeast Asia into 9.642 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to the Chao Phraya trunk stream, its northern tributaries (Ping, Wang, Yom, Nan) and the Mekong river network, applying exponential density attenuation beyond 12 km in dry terrace environments [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Claude2019Recent].
- Alluvial geomasking: binary and continuous weights identifying recent Quaternary alluvium, silt-renewed floodplains and backswamp depressions capable of sustaining wet-rice cultivation [@Claude2019Recent; @Taweethong2023Early].
- Topographic slope: penalising steep upland gradients in the Tenasserim, Daen Lao and Annamite ranges, while favouring flat alluvial plains, deltaic fan bluffs and intermontane valley floors [@Stark2020Landscapes].
- Hydrological accessibility: proximity to navigable coastal estuaries, tidal channels and canalized waterways that supported regional exchange and demographic nucleation [@Patnukao2024Tracing; @Tangtenglam2023Developing].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To avoid double counting between urban concentrations and surrounding agrarian populations, 850 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then distributed across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary smoothing algorithm harmonises density gradients across sub-regional frontiers, preventing artificial step discontinuities along watershed divides and historical administrative limits [@Thailand2020Brain].

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across early modern benchmarks, widening to +/- 15% during early historic and prehistoric horizons). In 1769AD, the regional total of 5,1M is bounded between 4,69M and 5,51M inhabitants. This uncertainty envelope accounts for variances in archaeological site area measurements, variable household occupancy multipliers and incomplete epigraphic preservation across different political epochs [@Murphy2015Many; @Michael1991Khamhaeng].

# Testing and Validation

## Archaeological Settlement Surveys and Inscription Records

Settlement locations and urban extents were validated through systematic spatial comparisons against published archaeological survey gazetteers, epigraphic compilations and aerial photography [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many]. GIS analyses conducted by Patnukao and colleagues on Dvaravati sites across central and peninsular Thailand demonstrated that moated sites correlate strongly with ancient river levees and natural spillways, confirming that early urban foundations were deliberately positioned to control seasonal flood discharge rather than constructed on random alluvial terrain [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Patnukao2024Tracing].

Epigraphic records provide chronological anchors for regional state foundations and monastic donations [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Murphy2015Many]. In Northeast Thailand and Central Laos, Murphy's quantitative analyses of Buddhist boundary stones (bai sema) and associated Mon and Sanskrit inscriptions demonstrate widespread monastic foundations during the seventh to eleventh centuries AD, establishing that secondary and tertiary centres formed dense religious networks prior to the expansion of Angkorian administrative control [@Murphy2015Many]. In northern Thailand, stone inscriptions from Sukhothai, Si Satchanalai and Chiang Mai record municipal water management works, royal tax exemptions and temple construction programmes, confirming the administrative capacity of thirteenth and fourteenth century Tai polities [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Thailand2024Promote].

## Bioarchaeological and Palaeoenvironmental Constraints

Palaeozoological investigations in the Chao Phraya central plain conducted by Claude and colleagues reveal significant environmental transformations and faunal turnover associated with late Holocene agricultural expansion [@Claude2019Recent]. Fossil turtle assemblages recovered from archaeological strata demonstrate that the central plain originally supported dense riverine swamps and gallery forests that were progressively cleared for wet-rice paddy fields between 500BC and 1500AD [@Claude2019Recent]. Local extinctions of wetland-adapted taxa coincide with the expansion of royal drainage canals and large-scale agrarian colonization during the Ayutthaya period [@Claude2019Recent; @Tangtenglam2023Developing].

Furthermore, archaeological excavation data from Bang Pakong Valley sites confirm continuous maritime interaction and metallurgical production spanning the first millennium BC and AD [@Taweethong2023Early]. Micro-botanical analyses of phytoliths and pollen cores demonstrate the dominance of domesticated *Oryza sativa* alongside managed fruit orchards (*Areca catechu*, *Cocos nucifera*), providing empirical constraints on pre-modern caloric carrying capacity [@Taweethong2023Early; @Thailand2020Basic].

In southern peninsular Thailand, spatial and demographic indicator surveys conducted across Songkhla, Pattani and Nakhon Si Thammarat demonstrate strong correlations between historic temple distribution, coastal sand-ridge geomorphology and ancient settlement longevity [@Patnukao2024Tracing; @Thailand2023Growth]. Archival research from the Songkhla educational service area and regional museum inventories documents continuous settlement stability around Lake Songkhla and along protected trans-isthmian river routes [@Thailand2025Research; @Thailand2020Active]. In agricultural hinterlands, local pedagogical documentation confirms that small rural settlements maintained distinct social structures that buffered communities against regional harvest shocks [@Thailand2025Effect; @Thailand2020Brain].

## Agrarian Technology and Wet-Rice Caloric Capacity

Demographic density across Mainland Southeast Asia was fundamentally constrained by rice cultivation regimes [@Thailand2020Basic]. Three primary agricultural systems coexisted across the region:
1. Deep-water floating rice: practiced in the low-lying central Chao Phraya depression, where floodwaters rose two to three metres during the monsoon season. Farmers broadcasted fast-elongating rice varieties that grew upward with rising floodwaters, requiring minimal land preparation and producing moderate yields with low labour inputs [@Claude2019Recent; @Tangtenglam2023Developing].
2. Bunded paddy with transplanting: practiced on river levees, alluvial fans and terrace slopes, where water levels could be regulated through field bunds and ditch diversion. This system required intensive seasonal labour for seedbed preparation, transplantation and weeding, but delivered caloric yields capable of sustaining 250 to 400 persons per square kilometre of cultivated land [@Thailand2020Basic; @Thailand2025Effect].
3. Intermontane canal irrigation (muang fai): deployed in northern valleys such as Chiang Mai, where bamboo and stone weirs diverted mountain streams into networks of earthen canals, allowing double-cropping and insulating valley populations against regional drought [@Thailand2020Basic; @Thailand2023Growth].

These agricultural adaptations allowed the Lower Chao Phraya basin to support dramatic demographic expansion during the Ayutthayan era without precipitating catastrophic Malthusian crises [@Thailand2020Basic; @Tangtenglam2023Developing].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger was constructed through an asymptotic multi-wave ingestion protocol designed to eliminate spatial omission biases:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official national gazetteers, municipal administrative records and census tables across Thailand and Laos, incorporating 527 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of archaeological excavation registers, epigraphic directories and historical monographs, adding 230 ancient and mediaeval centres.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill, foundation year verification and toponym harmonization, incorporating 93 early historic and provincial centres.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits across all six divisions, resulting in zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 1.034 candidate localities were audited: 850 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 184 were excluded (predominantly duplicate survey aliases within 2,2 km or non-habitation features).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Dynamics

The demographic evolution of the Chao Phraya, Mekong and Peninsular realms across more than two millennia reveals a trajectory characterized by steady prehistoric growth, accelerated early historic urbanisation, northern Tai expansion and climactic early modern maritime integration (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Late Prehistoric and Iron Age Communities (500BC to 500AD)

During the late first millennium BC and early centuries AD, regional population grew from 950k in 500BC (yielding an aggregate density of 121,27 persons per 100 km²) to 1,45M in 500AD (185,1 persons per 100 km²). Settlement was concentrated along perennial river confluences, piedmont fans and coastal estuaries where seasonal flooding facilitated rice farming and iron working [@Taweethong2023Early]. The Lower Chao Phraya accommodated 285k people in 500BC rising to 435k in 500AD, while the Khorat Plateau accommodated 171k rising to 261k, anchored by dense moated villages along the Mun and Chi drainages [@Murphy2015Many]. Coastal trade networks along the Kra Isthmus began funneling Indian glass beads, Roman coins and Han Chinese ceramics into local chiefdoms [@Patnukao2024Tracing].

### Dvaravati Urbanism and Early Historic Mon-Khmer Polities (500AD to 1000AD)

Between 500AD and 1000AD, regional population advanced from 1,45M to 2,15M inhabitants (274,45 persons per 100 km²). This epoch witnessed the flowering of the Dvaravati civilization across the central plain and the expansion of Khmer provincial outposts across the Khorat Plateau [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many]. Mon-speaking cities surrounded by oval earthen ramparts and moats emerged at Nakhon Pathom, Ku Bua, U Thong, Lopburi and Si Mahosot. Buddhist monasteries functioned as demographic and economic engines, mobilizing surplus rice and craft labour [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many]. By 1000AD, the Lower Chao Phraya supported 645k people, the Khorat Plateau housed 387k, Lan Na supported 322,5k, the Upper Chao Phraya accommodated 301k, Lan Xang housed 279,5k and the Peninsular Isthmus reached 215k.

### Northern Tai Migration and Territorial Consolidation (1000AD to 1350AD)

The period between 1000AD and 1350AD witnessed profound demographic reorganisation as Tai-speaking populations established autonomous polities across the northern valleys and upper alluvial plains [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Stark2020Landscapes]. Regional population climbed from 2,15M in 1000AD to 2,95M by 1300AD (376,57 persons per 100 km²). Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai emerged as prominent urban centres along the Yom River, developing sophisticated hydraulic networks and large-scale Sangkhalok ceramic manufacturing [@Michael1991Khamhaeng]. In the north, King Mangrai founded Chiang Mai in 1296AD, consolidating Lan Na into an enduring political confederation [@Stark2020Landscapes; @Thailand2024Strategies]. By 1300AD, Lan Na accommodated 442,5k inhabitants, the Upper Chao Phraya supported 413k, and the Lower Chao Phraya concentrated 885k people.

### Ayutthayan Hegemony and Early Modern Maritime Integration (1350AD to 1769AD)

The foundation of Ayutthaya in 1351AD initiated four centuries of centralized state formation, intensive canal construction and commercial expansion [@Tangtenglam2023Developing]. Regional population expanded from 2,95M in 1300AD to 3,9M in 1500AD, reaching 4,75M in 1650AD and attaining 5,1M by 1769AD (yielding an aggregate density of 651,02 persons per 100 km²). Ayutthaya developed into a cosmopolitan hydraulic capital, surrounded by extensive rice-producing hinterlands linked by royal transport canals [@Tangtenglam2023Developing; @Claude2019Recent].

Maritime commerce linked Ayutthaya to international trading ports across Eurasia [@Patnukao2024Tracing; @Taweethong2023Early]. Overland transpeninsular portage routes connected Mergui and Tenasserim on the Bay of Bengal with the Gulf of Thailand, enabling merchants to bypass the pirate-infested waters of the Malacca Strait. Royal trading fleets exported sapanwood, deerskins, tin, ivory and aromatic resins to China and Japan, importing silks, porcelain and copper cash that stimulated domestic monetization [@Tangtenglam2023Developing].

Simultaneously, Lan Xang unified the middle Mekong basin from Luang Prabang and Vientiane, while maritime sultanates and principalities flourished along the Kra Isthmus at Nakhon Si Thammarat, Songkhla and Patani [@Murphy2015Many; @Patnukao2024Tracing]. Despite repeated military conflicts with the Toungoo and Konbaung dynasties of Burma, concluding with the catastrophic fall of Ayutthaya in 1767AD, demographic recovery occurred rapidly under King Taksin at Thonburi, preserving the agrarian foundation of the Lower Chao Phraya basin.

The urban settlement hierarchy exhibited four distinct structural tiers:
1. Primary metropolitan capitals (> 100k inhabitants): Ayutthaya (261,71k peak in 1500AD, 240,94k in 1650AD) and Thonburi (249,44k in 1769AD). These primate centres coordinated inter-regional trade, royal administration, hydraulic engineering works and military mobilizations [@Tangtenglam2023Developing].
2. Major regional and provincial capitals (30k to 100k inhabitants): Chiang Mai (52,15k peak in 1500AD), Samut Sakhon (55,75k peak), Khlong Luang (50,89k peak), Vientiane (43,53k peak in 1769AD), Nakhon Sawan (43,37k peak), Nakhon Pathom (38,38k peak), Kanchanaburi (37,18k peak), Sukhothai (31,99k peak in 1300AD) and Nakhon Ratchasima (30,84k peak in 1769AD). These walled centres commanded river junctions and frontier trade corridors [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Murphy2015Many].
3. Secondary administrative and craft centres (15k to 30k inhabitants): Kamphaeng Phet (29,77k peak), Lat Krabang (29,42k peak), Bang Lamung (27,47k peak), Khon Kaen (27,27k peak), Luang Prabang (26,75k peak), Si Racha (26,72k peak), Bang Sao Thong (25,78k peak), Sa Kaeo (23,38k peak) and Prachuap Khiri Khan (22,96k peak). These localities served as provincial garrisons, market nodes and ceramic centres [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Taweethong2023Early].
4. Tertiary market towns and agricultural hamlets (< 15k inhabitants): hundreds of moated villages, riverine landing points and upland farming communities catalogued throughout the six divisions [@Murphy2015Many; @Patnukao2024Tracing].

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis across early Thailand and Laos remains subject to several empirical constraints:
1. Taphonomic degradation of perishable architecture: pre-modern domestic dwellings and defensive structures across Mainland Southeast Asia were constructed almost exclusively from timber, bamboo and thatch raised on stilts. Only religious monuments (stupas, viharas, prangs) were built from permanent brick and laterite, obscuring the physical footprints of commoner residential sectors [@Patnukao2017Dvaravati; @Tangtenglam2023Developing].
2. Alluvial sedimentation and delta progradation: dynamic flooding along the Chao Phraya trunk stream has buried ancient Dvaravati and early historic strata beneath metres of heavy clay and silt, making systematic subsurface detection difficult without mechanized coring [@Claude2019Recent; @Taweethong2023Early].
3. Loss of archival records: the comprehensive sack and burning of Ayutthaya by Konbaung Burmese forces in April 1767 destroyed royal administrative registries, tax records and monastic chronicles, compelling demographic researchers to rely upon foreign diplomatic accounts, surviving stone inscriptions and comparative archaeological estimates [@Tangtenglam2023Developing; @Michael1991Khamhaeng].
4. Shifting political boundaries and muang autonomy: the mandala structure of pre-modern Tai and Lao states meant that peripheral principalities frequently shifted allegiance between rival courts, complicating the boundary demarcation of sub-regional demographic envelopes [@Murphy2015Many; @Thailand2024Strategies].

# Conclusion

The early Tai principalities, Sukhothai, the Ayutthayan kingdom and the Lao realm of Lan Xang sustained a fourfold population expansion from 950k inhabitants in 500BC to 5,1M in 1769AD across 783.386 km² of territory. This historical demographic development was underpinned by the progressive canalization and agricultural colonization of the Chao Phraya delta, the expansion of community weir irrigation across northern intermontane valleys, and the integration of riverine capitals into international maritime trade networks.

From initial iron-age farming villages and Dvaravati monastic centres to the cosmopolitan hydraulic metropolis of Ayutthaya and the riverine kingdom of Lan Xang, regional societies developed resilient institutional structures capable of absorbing periodic warfare, seasonal droughts and flood pulses. By grounding demographic trajectories in georeferenced archaeological settlements and environmental covariates, MANDALA provides a consistent spatial foundation for understanding the demographic roots of pre-modern Mainland Southeast Asian civilization.
